Open work on the design language
================================

Deferred deliberately. Each of these is something we looked at, decided was
worth doing, and decided was not worth doing badly first.


1. Reordering: keep the dragged element visible
-----------------------------------------------
Status: done.
Where:  UI.lift in design_language.js, used by BEHAVIORS.reorder and
        BEHAVIORS.board; .is-lifted / .is-settling / .drag-gap in the CSS.

The row is now lifted out of flow and carried by the pointer, with a dashed
gap left where it was picked up, auto-scroll on every scroller the pointer
reaches the edge of, and a short settle on drop. The drop line stayed: it
marks a position BETWEEN two rows, which a floating row cannot.

Three things worth not undoing:

(a) The real element is lifted, NOT a clone. A clone has to be kept in sync
    with styling it cannot see — this kit resolves surface fills from nesting
    depth, and most applications style rows by ancestor — so a clone parked
    at the end of <body> paints differently from the row it stands in for,
    silently. Lifting in place keeps every selector that matched it matching,
    and keeps its focus, listeners and pointer capture.

(b) The gap is a neutral .drag-gap, not a copy of the element's classes. A
    placeholder wearing .board-card or .sortable-item is counted as one by
    every query in the file, including ones not written yet.

(c) Auto-scroll acts on what is under the POINTER, not on what the element
    was lifted out of. Those are the same thing in a list and different the
    moment a card leaves its column, which is how this was got wrong first
    time: dragging into a second column scrolled the first one. The scroll
    chain is rebuilt from elementsFromPoint whenever the element under the
    pointer changes.

Off by default for nobody; data-drag-proxy="off" on the component or any
ancestor turns it off, and the nearest one wins so a nested component can
turn it back on. Off falls back to the older drop-lines-and-a-faded-row.
UI.lift.edge / .speed / .settle are the thresholds.


2. Kanban board: the same problem
---------------------------------
Status: done, with (1) and by the same code.
Where:  patterns.html #board, BEHAVIORS.board in design_language.js

The board shares UI.lift rather than having its own. What is genuinely the
board's own is still the board's: the column a card is headed for, and a
second axis to scroll. Each axis is claimed by the first scroller that
actually moves on it, so a pointer in the corner scrolls a column down and
the board sideways at once, and a column that has hit its end hands the push
outward instead of swallowing it.


3. type="week" has no component
-------------------------------
Status: deliberate, documented on forms.html #types.
Where:  BEHAVIORS.picker in design_language.js

Every other upgradeable input type (number, date, time, datetime-local, month,
color) gets the kit's own picker by default. Week passes through to the
browser on purpose: ISO week numbering has its own year boundaries, and a week
picker that is merely plausible is worse than the browser's, which is at least
correct. It gets a component when it gets the week math.


4. Material Icons is a placeholder
----------------------------------
Status: deliberate. See ICONS.txt for the whole story.

Self-hosted, so nothing reaches a third-party host, but it is not final art
and is not part of this design language.

5. Two ordering traps that already bit once
-------------------------------------------
Status: fixed, recorded so they are not reintroduced.

(a) BEHAVIORS that GENERATE markup must run before the behaviors that wire
    that markup up. `picker` creates [data-popover] triggers and `popover` is
    what binds them; declared in the wrong order, every generated trigger was
    created just after the only pass that would have bound it. The fields
    looked perfect and clicking did nothing, with no error anywhere. init()
    now runs an explicit GENERATORS list first so position in the object
    cannot bring this back.

(b) Dispatch on the type ATTRIBUTE, never on input.type. A browser that does
    not implement an input type reports .type as "text" — Firefox does this
    for month and week — so a property-based switch upgrades a field in one
    browser and silently skips it in another.

Both of these failed silently and neither showed up in a console. Test a
picker by CLICKING its trigger, not by calling UI.openPopover(): the API call
bypasses exactly the binding that was broken.

6. scrollIntoView is almost never what a panel wants
-----------------------------------------------------
Status: fixed in the time picker, and now everywhere it mattered.

scrollIntoView scrolls EVERY scrollable ancestor up to the document, not just
the nearest one. The time picker called it with { block: 'center' } on the
chosen row of each of its three columns, on every render, and a render ran on
every pick — so choosing AM hauled the whole page up, then down, then up again
under the pointer. Both the time picker and the date+time picker had it.

To center something inside one scroller, set that scroller's scrollTop from
bounding rects. It cannot reach past the element you name. That is what
UI.keepInView does, and it is also the keyboard half of a lift: an arrow key
moves the real element, so it needs no proxy, but the scroller still has to
follow it. The board's keyboard move used scrollIntoView and now uses this —
moving a card between columns was nudging the page.

The remaining scrollIntoView calls in the file all use { block: 'nearest' },
which only scrolls when the target is actually out of view and moves the
minimum to fix it. That one is usually fine.

7. Lifted dragging: what is not done
------------------------------------
Status: open, and none of it blocks anything.

(a) Touch is wired the same way as mouse and pen — it is all pointer events —
    but it has not been driven on a real touch screen, only with a pointer.
    The thing to check is the hand-off between touch-action: none and the
    auto-scroll, which are two different ways of saying "this gesture is not
    a page scroll".

(b) A lift inside a transformed or contained ancestor anchors to that
    ancestor rather than to the viewport, because that is what position:
    fixed does there. The geometry is handled; the clipping is not, so a row
    dragged out of such a container is clipped at its edge. No component in
    the kit is in that position today.

(c) Nothing reorders ACROSS two separate lists. The board crosses columns
    because one behavior owns all of them. Two independent [data-reorder]
    lists exchanging rows needs a shared drop target, which is a different
    question from carrying the row and should not be bolted onto it.

8. Custom scrollbars
--------------------
Status: done.
Where:  BEHAVIORS.scrollbar and the Scrollbars module in design_language.js;
        the Scrollbars block in the CSS; the --scrollbar-* tokens.

The native bar is hidden everywhere and the kit draws its own, because the
native one cannot be made to match across engines: ::-webkit-scrollbar reaches
its shape in Chrome and Safari, Firefox exposes a two-keyword width and a pair
of colors, and a touch platform discards both for its own fading overlay.

Five things worth not undoing:

(a) The bars are NOT children of the scroller. They are fixed elements parked
    at the end of <body>, or of the floating surface the scroller sits on so
    they share its stacking context, and placed from the scroller's rect. A
    child would be far cheaper to position and would have broken what
    :last-child, :nth-child and :empty select inside every scroller in the
    kit. .editor-surface settles it on its own: it is contenteditable, and an
    injected node there is something the writer can put a caret in and delete.

(b) The gutter is real padding, not an overlay. The native bar took its width
    out of the content box; reserve() puts the same width back as
    padding-inline-end. That is why switching from native to drawn reflowed
    nothing.

    NEVER read that padding back out of getComputedStyle while our own gutter
    could still be on the element. The first version cleared the inline
    padding and read the computed value in the same tick, trusting the read
    to flush the clear first. On a 120Hz Firefox, where a ResizeObserver was
    driving measure() every frame, it did not flush: the read returned the
    gutter that had just been cleared, reserve() counted it as authored
    padding, and added a second gutter on top. Ten pixels a frame, about 840
    a second; the page was past fifteen thousand pixels wide within seconds,
    and every scroller on it grew with the document. It never once reproduced
    under automation in either engine, at any viewport or device scale,
    because it depends entirely on flush timing — it only showed up on the
    machine it showed up on.

    So the authored padding is measured once, at a moment the element is
    known to be clean, and cached. The cache is dropped when the viewport
    changes, which is what moves a breakpoint; re-measuring then deliberately
    takes two frames, one to take ours off and the next to read what is left.
    The regression test for this fakes a computed value that lags the inline
    write by one frame: the old code runs away to 1000px under it in fifty
    passes, this one does not move off 10px.

(c) Measuring and drawing are separate passes. draw() runs on every scroll
    frame and only reads rects and offsets; measure() reads computed styles
    and rewrites padding and runs only when something structural changed. On
    interactions.html, with 23 scrollers, this holds a continuous scroll at
    8.4ms median with no frame over 32ms.

(d) Scrollers are found by reading the kit's own stylesheet for every rule
    that makes something scroll, so a new overflow rule needs no matching edit
    in the JS. Two things that list cannot reach, and both were real bugs
    before they were handled: a textarea and a <select multiple> scroll by the
    UA stylesheet, which is not in document.styleSheets; and a file:// page
    cannot read its own sheet at all in Chrome, where cssRules throws
    SecurityError. The first is a short explicit list, the second falls back
    to asking every element in the document, which costs 1-2ms on the heaviest
    page here. Do not reintroduce the "skip anything that already fits"
    optimisation in that sweep: it measured as a tenth of a millisecond and it
    misses the box that is declared scrollable but has not overflowed yet,
    which is precisely the one that has to be claimed before its content
    arrives.

(e) The thumb FILLS the gutter and is only drawn narrower, using a
    transparent border and background-clip rather than a width. That is a hit
    area decision, not a cosmetic one. A 6px thumb centered in a 10px gutter
    leaves two dead pixels down each side, and the pair on the outer side sits
    at the edge of the window — on a maximized window, the edge of the screen,
    which is the one target a pointer can be thrown at without aiming because
    it cannot be overshot. Landing there was hitting the track and paging,
    which is the opposite of what a thrown pointer is asking for. Do not
    reintroduce a width on the thumb.

What is not done:

(f) It has not been driven on a real touch screen, only with a pointer. The
    gutter is reserved on touch as well, where the platform's own bar would
    have been an overlay taking no space. That is deliberate, for one answer
    everywhere, but it is a visible difference from the platform, and 10px is
    still thin for a finger. If it needs to be fatter there, --scrollbar-size
    is one token and the thumb follows it.

(g) The page's bar deliberately sits under the scrim, at --layer-scrollbar-page
    350, below --layer-overlay. Once a dialog has locked the document there is
    nothing left for that bar to scroll, and a bar left bright over a dimmed
    page reads as a control that still works. A native bar would have stayed
    lit. If that ever reads as wrong, it is one token.

(h) The thumb is not focusable and takes no keys. Neither does a native
    scrollbar — the scroller itself is what the keyboard drives, and that is
    untouched — so this is a decision rather than a gap, but it is the kind of
    decision worth having written down.
